pr_body:
Use read/write locking on Windows

    Fixes #13914

    The "SRWLock" synchronization primitive is available in Windows Vista
    and later.  CRYPTO_THREAD functions now use SRWLock functions when the
    target operating system supports them.

##### Checklist

- [x] documentation is added or updated
- [x] `test_encoder_decoder_legacy.t` currently hangs. Either #14319 or #14171 will fix.

issue_context.title: Read/Write locking on Windows / FIPS
issue_context.body:
My company is currently using version 1.0.2 on Windows. We recently discovered a performance issue when running our product in FIPS mode. Debugging proved lock contention within hashing functions, essentially single-threading password validation throughout all threads in our product. 

After some analysis, we concluded that the locking callbacks we provided to OpenSSL through `CRYPTO_set_locking_callback` were insufficient, checking only the `CRYPTO_LOCK` and `CRYPTO_UNLOCK` bits and using a Windows mutex to synchronize.

So we quickly replaced the callbacks to handle the additional `CRYPTO_READ` and `CRYPTO_WRITE` bits and use an [SRWLock](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sync/slim-reader-writer--srw--locks) primitive for synchronization. This resolved the issue and we're shipping a patch ASAP.

Follow-up searching turned up another OpenSSL 1.0.2 user [who had encountered a similar problem](https://mta.openssl.org/pipermail/openssl-users/2015-April/001288.html). Their solution was to ignore the FIPS-related mutexes after enabling FIPS had completed.

This raises some issues with our upgrade path. When FIPS is available/possible in version 3.0 we would like to upgrade, but it seems as though we would need read/write locking support on Windows to avoid this performance issue.

OpenSSL now (since 1.1.1?) implements its own thread synchronization. The [current Windows implementation](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/crypto/threads_win.c) uses a `CriticalSection` with no checks for the `CRYPTO_READ` and `CRYPTO_WRITE` bits. It appears that the [threading callbacks have been removed](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/3aa7212e0a4fd1533c8a28b8587dd8b022f3a66f/include/openssl/crypto.h.in#L255), so we would not be able to "specifically ignore" the FIPS mutexes.

Should we anticipate running into the same issue with FIPS on version 3.0?
If so, is there interest (aside from myself) in implementing read/write locking for Windows?

Thanks!
comments:
> OpenSSL now (since 1.1.1?)

Since 1.1.0.  As you've discovered, we ripped out the old locking callbacks and replaced that with built in lock functionality instead, which also allowed us to have locks with much finer granularity (the pre-1.1.0 locks were much more "global").

From your text, it looks like you may have found a bug!  Our locking interface does indeed allow read and write locking...  if we don't support that on Windows (which is what it sounds like from your description), then it needs to be fixed.  PR welcome.

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-initializesrwlock

- Vista+ 
- Server 2008+

Looking over the [pthread implementation](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/crypto/threads_pthread.c), using the `USE_RWLOCK` macro along with an `#if (WINVER >= 0x600)` could prevent use of SRWLock APIs prior to Vista and 2008. 

However, `threads_pthread.c` uses a recursive mutex:

```
    pthread_mutexattr_init(&attr);
    #if defined(__TANDEM) && defined(_SPT_MODEL_)
      pthread_mutexattr_setkind_np(&attr,MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP);
    #else
      pthread_mutexattr_settype(&attr, PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE);
    #endif
```

[MS documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sync/slim-reader-writer--srw--locks) states that SRWLock does not support recursive locking:

> An SRW lock is the size of a pointer. The advantage is that it is fast to update the lock state. The disadvantage is that very little state information can be stored, so SRW locks do not detect incorrect recursive use in shared mode. In addition, a thread that owns an SRW lock in shared mode cannot upgrade its ownership of the lock to exclusive mode.

SRWLock is appealing in its simplicity and performance, but something else would have to be used if the rest of OpenSSL assumes support for recursive or upgraded locks.

Is recursive locking and/or lock upgrading *required* by the rest of OpenSSL, or was it implemented this way just as a precaution?

> Is recursive locking and/or lock upgrading a required by the rest of OpenSSL, or was it implemented this way just as a precaution?

Unfortunately I don't know. I'm not aware of anywhere that we do this recursively...but I can't say for sure that we don't.

One way to do a quick sanity check would be remove those lines, build, and see if any test hangs.  That wouldn't be comprehensive of course.

I would be very surprised if we used them, or if we did read-upgradeto-write stuff atomically.

> read-upgradeto-write stuff atomically.

The read-to-write thing is actually undefined with pthreads, so we shouldn't be doing that. But recursively taking a read lock *is* allowed.
Yes, I know recursion is allowed. I recall arguing against it when this work was done.I still would be very surprised if openssl does it, given the way it uses locks.
If we find we're not using it, I'd suggest removing it for the pthreads implementation. There's no point in pthreads allowing it and Windows not. That just hides any problems.

> One way to do a quick sanity check would be remove those lines, build, and see if any test hangs. That wouldn't be comprehensive of course.

[pthread_mutexattr_settype](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/pthread_mutexattr_settype.html) has a `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK` type that could be used to detect recursive locks. It looks like the calling code, though, would have to check the return value for every lock/unlock. I'm unsure if that is done universally.
the `CRYPTO_` locks calls  could do it an assert.  I will whip up a PR.

@VeeFu would you be willing to pull together a PR for making the necessary changes for Windows rw locks?

> would you be willing to pull together a PR for making the necessary changes for Windows rw lock

Yes, it is on my list. I won't be able to get to it for another week.

My product shipped with the SRWLock callbacks in 1.0.2 about three weeks ago. So far, only one customer has reported issues. The issue does, however, raise a couple questions that need answering before we're totally confident that SRWLock is the best choice going forward

I'm not sure if SRWLock can fit in the existing thread locking API.

Microsoft's SRWLock has four functions, lock and unlock in shared and exclusive mode
* `AcquireSRWLockShared`
* `AcquireSRWLockExclusive`
* `ReleaseSRWLockShared`
* `ReleaseSRWLockExclusive`

Unfortunately, `crypto/threads_*.c` files only expose three functions
* `CRYPTO_THREAD_read_lock`
* `CRYPTO_THREAD_write_lock`
* `CRYPTO_THREAD_unlock`

pthreads locking API only has a single 'unlock' function, usable from either the 'read' or 'write'-locked state. SRWLock requires matching calls to 'exclusive lock' and 'exclusive unlock'. Likewise for 'shared lock' and 'shared unlock'.
